Arbelos Rect

GeometryCirclesArea
What it shows: A big half-circle with two smaller ones inside it, and a four-sided shape drawn between them.
How to play: Drag C along the bottom line or D on the big curve. Focus a point and use the arrow keys to nudge it, or press a button. Tick the boxes to show names or hints.
Look for the math

Move C along the bottom line. The four-sided shape CEDF tilts and changes size, yet two things never fail: it stays a rectangle, and its far edge keeps touching both small half-circles. Why?

The upright through C

Write AC = a and CB = b. D sits on the big semicircle, so the upright CD is the geometric mean of the two pieces of the diameter:

CD² = AC × CB, so CD = √(ab).

The applet finds D with exactly this square root. Our logic test checks it at 1001 positions of C and against the applet's own formula at 2000 more.

Why CEDF is a rectangle

An angle drawn across a full diameter is a right angle (Thales' theorem). So AEC, ADB and CFB are all right angles. These make EC perpendicular to ED, and make the opposite sides match in pairs: CEDF is a parallelogram with a right corner, hence a rectangle. Its two diagonals are equal, so EF = CD = √(ab) at every position. That is the page's first claim, and the test checks all of it.

The common tangent

Let Oa be the middle of AC. The triangle AOaE has two equal sides, so its two angles at A and E match. Chasing those angles through the rectangle shows that OaE is perpendicular to EF. The same argument at the other circle gives ObF perpendicular to EF. A line perpendicular to a radius at its end is a tangent, so EF touches both small semicircles. The page's remark adds another neat equality: if O is the middle of the rectangle, then OE = OC. The test checks the angle chain, both tangencies and that equality.

The area equality

From CD² = ab comes the area result familiar from the companion page about the area of the arbelos: the half-circle on AB minus the two half-circles on AC and CB has area

π(a+b)²/8 − πa²/8 − πb²/8 = πab/4 = πCD²/4.

That last number is exactly the area of the circle with CD as its diameter. The rectangle's own area is ab × CD / (a+b). The logic test confirms all three area formulas at 1001 positions and 2000 random ones.

About the original

The Java applet let you drag only C along the bottom line; D was computed above it. Here you can also drag D along the big arc, which sets the same position. Its three checkboxes (names, hint 1, hint 2) are kept. One harmless leftover is not copied: the applet's "about" text described a regular polygon demonstration. The page's two numbered claims are reproduced exactly, and no behaviour was dropped.

Press C in the middle, then tick both hints. Drag C towards A and watch the rectangle keeps its right corners while EF keeps touching both arcs.
